introduction-the-heavy-crown.core: A leader serialises decisions (who writes, who runs the cron job, who owns a shard), simplifying coordination. But leadership is dangerous: a node can believe it's still leader after it has been replaced (pauses, partitions), so systems must make stale leaders harmless. Elect via consensus (etcd, ZooKeeper, Raft), and protect resources with fencing.

first_principles.problem: Two instances of a scheduler both think they're leader and run every job twice.
truths: Nodes can't know they've been deposed.

analogy.title: A crown that can be secretly passed on
analogy.story: If the old king doesn't know he's been replaced, his orders must be ignored by the guards.
analogy.breaks: Kings get told; paused processes literally can't notice time passed.

example.title: Scheduler leadership
flow: Candidates race to create lease key in etcd
Winner renews every 5 s with TTL 15 s
Workers reject jobs with older terms

check.q: Why can't a leader simply know it has been replaced?
check.a: It may be paused or partitioned and has no way to observe the election that happened meanwhile.

the-physics-of-split-brain.core: Split-brain arises from asymmetric knowledge: during a partition, a minority-side leader keeps acting while the majority elects a new one, or a GC/VM pause freezes a leader past its lease. Clocks and timeouts can't fully prevent it, because the old leader doesn't experience the passage of time. Only majority quorums plus fencing at the resource make it safe.

first_principles.problem: A 40-second GC pause lets a stale primary write after failover, corrupting data.
truths: Pauses are invisible to the paused process.
Only the resource sees both writers.

analogy.title: Rip Van Winkle waking and giving orders
analogy.story: He thinks no time has passed; everyone else knows things have changed.
analogy.breaks: Rip notices his beard; processes have no such cue.

example.title: Pause timeline
flow: Leader A holds lease to t=30
A pauses at t=25 for 40 s
A wakes at t=65, believes lease valid → writes

check.q: Why can't leases alone prevent split-brain?
check.a: A paused leader may wake after its lease expired and act without realising, so the resource must reject it.

fencing-tokens-the-zombie-defense.core: A fencing token is a monotonically increasing number (e.g. the lease revision or Raft term) issued with each grant of leadership or lock. Every write to the protected resource includes the token, and the resource rejects any token lower than the highest it has seen. Zombie leaders with old tokens are blocked no matter how long they were paused.

first_principles.problem: A lock holder pauses, its lock expires, another client takes the lock, and both write to storage.
truths: Resources can remember the highest seen.
derivation: Get **token with lock/lease** (etcd revision, ZK zxid).
Use **conditional writes** where storage lacks native support.

analogy.title: Numbered parking permits
analogy.story: The car park only accepts the latest permit number, so old permits are useless even if they look valid.
analogy.breaks: Permits are checked by attendants; resources must implement the check.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Zombie with token 33 rejected after token 34 was used.

check.q: Who must check fencing tokens: the leader or the resource?
check.a: The resource (storage or service), because the stale leader can't know it's stale.

lease-based-election-and-clock-skew.core: Leases grant leadership for a time period, renewed periodically. They rely on bounded clock drift: the leader must stop acting before the lease expires by its own clock, with a safety margin, while others wait the full duration plus drift before taking over. Pauses and clock jumps break naive leases, so use monotonic clocks, margins and fencing together.

first_principles.problem: A leader with a slow clock keeps acting after others think its lease expired.
truths: Pauses stop renewal but not belief.

analogy.title: Borrowing a meeting room until 3 pm by your watch
analogy.story: If your watch is slow you overstay, so you leave five minutes early and others wait five minutes extra.
analogy.breaks: People notice others waiting; processes don't notice anything during pauses.

example.title: Lease timing
flow: Leader acts only until 13 s since grant (monotonic)

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Overlap avoided under bounded drift; fencing covers pauses.

check.q: Why should a lease holder stop acting before the lease's nominal expiry?
check.a: To account for clock drift between itself and others, avoiding overlap with a new leader.
